title: The Hermes Skills Guide: Author Playbooks Your AI Actually Follows
description: Learn what Hermes skills are, how to read and judge a SKILL.md, and how to author, validate, and publish your own skills to the marketplace.

lessons.title: Skills Are Playbooks, Not Prompts
lessons.bodyMd:
## Skills Are Playbooks, Not Prompts

Imagine you are training a new team member. For simple questions you answer on the spot. For anything complex, you hand them a playbook: the exact steps, the traps to avoid, and what "done" looks like. That is what a Hermes skill is for an AI model.

A Hermes skill is a folder containing a single file called `SKILL.md`. That file is a Markdown document written for an AI to read, not for a human to browse. It teaches any compatible AI model (Claude, GPT-4o, Gemini, Cursor, and others) how to perform a specific job: the commands to run, the order to run them in, the decisions to make, and how to verify the result.

The key word is reusable. Without a skill, every AI session starts from zero. You explain the same workflow again and again, and the model gets it mostly right but with drift. With a skill, the workflow is captured once, reviewed, and then loaded identically in every future session. The model follows the same useful discipline every time.

## The 369-Skill Marketplace

The LetsVibeAI marketplace hosts hundreds of these playbooks covering automation, development, marketing, research, and more. When you install a skill, you are not installing software in the traditional sense. You are giving your AI a new capability on demand: it reads the playbook and behaves accordingly.

Think of it this way:

- **Without skills:** you type a long, detailed prompt, hope the model remembers every nuance, and correct its mistakes.
- **With skills:** you type "set up my dev environment" or "research this topic," the model loads the right playbook, and follows a tested procedure.

Skills do not replace your judgment. They replace repetition. You still decide what to build; the skill handles the how, so the model does not have to guess.

## What You Will Learn in This Guide

By the end of these five chapters you will be able to:

1. Explain what a Hermes skill is and how AI models discover and use them.
2. Read any `SKILL.md` and know exactly what each part does.
3. Judge the quality of a skill before you install it.
4. Write your own skill from a workflow you already know.
5. Package and publish it to the marketplace so others can use it.

No programming is required. The skill format is plain Markdown with a small YAML header. If you can write a README, you can write a skill.

lessons.title: How AI Agents Use Skills
lessons.bodyMd:
## How a Model Finds the Right Skill

Skills are not magic. They work through a simple mechanism: a searchable description plus a document body.

Every skill folder contains `SKILL.md`, and every `SKILL.md` starts with a short header called frontmatter. The most important field in that header is `description`, a one or two sentence summary that starts with the phrase "Use when...". For example:

```yaml
description: "Use when you need to install and manage Python packages in the Hermes Agent virtual environment."
```

When you ask the model a question, the agent framework searches the descriptions of all installed skills for a match against your request. The model does not read all 369 skills at once; that would be far too expensive and slow. It reads only the descriptions, picks the skill whose description best matches your task, and then loads the full body of that one skill into its context.

This is why the description matters so much. It is the skill's storefront sign. A vague description means the skill never gets picked up, no matter how good the body is.

## What Happens After the Skill Loads

Once loaded, the body of `SKILL.md` becomes part of the model's working instructions for that task. A good body reads like a recipe with a verification step:

1. **When to use:** the triggers that should call this skill, and just as importantly, the situations where it should NOT be used.
2. **The procedure:** ordered steps with checkable completion criteria ("how do I know this step is done?").
3. **Common pitfalls:** the mistakes people and models repeatedly make, with fixes.
4. **Verification checklist:** a list the model runs through before declaring victory.

The skill does not hardcode the model's output. The model still reasons, adapts, and handles surprises. The skill simply constrains the process so the model follows a proven path instead of inventing one from scratch.

## LLM-Agnostic by Design

One of the core ideas behind Hermes is that skills should not be tied to one AI product. A well-written skill teaches any model the same workflow. That is why skill descriptions in the marketplace name multiple models ("instructs any AI model: Claude, GPT-4o, Gemini, Cursor") and avoid product-specific jargon where possible.

In practice this means:

- Skills reference standard commands and files, not hidden product features.
- When a product-specific tool is needed (like the Hermes `skill_manage` tool for editing in-repo skills), the skill names it explicitly rather than assuming.
- Skills say what behavior should change when they load, which is a universal concept regardless of the model.

## The Mental Model to Keep

If you remember one picture from this lesson, make it this one:

**Description = the trigger.** Short, searchable, starts with "Use when".

**Body = the playbook.** The steps, traps, and checks the model follows once triggered.

**Marketplace = the library.** Hundreds of playbooks, each installing on demand, each teaching your AI something new.

lessons.title: Why Skills Matter
lessons.bodyMd:
## The Problem Skills Solve: Drift

Every AI conversation starts fresh. The model is smart but forgetful: it has no memory of the workflow you perfected last week unless you paste it in again. And even when you do paste it, the details drift. A flag is forgotten here, a verification step skipped there. The result is work that is right on the surface but wrong in the details.

This is the predictability problem. You do not need the model to produce identical output every run; that is impossible and not even desirable. You need it to reliably follow the same useful discipline: check the same preconditions, run the same verification, refuse to skip the same step.

Skills solve drift by making the discipline explicit and loadable. The procedure lives in a file that can be reviewed, versioned, and improved. Each time the model follows it, you get the benefit of every fix you have ever made to it.

## The Second Problem: Token Cost

There is also a cost argument. AI models charge (or budget) by tokens read. A long workflow pasted into every chat costs you tokens every single time, and it crowds out the actual task in the model's working memory.

Skills use progressive disclosure to keep this cheap:

- The model reads only **descriptions** every turn. These are one to two sentences each, tiny.
- It loads the **full body** of only the one skill it needs.
- Bulky reference material lives in the skill's `references/`, `templates/`, or `scripts/` folders and is loaded only when the task calls for it.

A 369-skill library costs almost nothing to keep installed because the model only pays for what it uses.

## Why This Matters to You as a Beginner

You are learning to build with AI at a moment when "using AI" is becoming "managing a team of AI agents." Skills are the management layer. They are how you:

- **Teach your agent once** instead of typing the same instructions in every chat.
- **Capture expertise** you develop (your deployment checklist, your research routine) so future-you benefits.
- **Share with others** through the marketplace, turning personal workflow into community value.
- **Trust automation** because each skill carries its own verification checklist.

Patrick built the Hermes framework out of exactly this need: too many workflows were living in his head and in chat history, and every new session meant re-teaching them. Skills were the answer. You are now learning the system that powers the whole LetsVibeAI marketplace.

## What Comes Next

In Chapter 2 you will open a real `SKILL.md` and take it apart piece by piece: the frontmatter, the body sections, and the conventions that make skills in the marketplace feel consistent. By the end you will be able to read any skill like a spec sheet.

lessons.title: The Frontmatter Block
lessons.bodyMd:
## The Two Parts of Every SKILL.md

Open any skill and you will see the same shape:

```
---
name: hermes-dependencies
description: "Use when you need to install and manage Python packages..."
version: 1.1.0
author: Hermes Agent
license: MIT
---
# Hermes Dependencies
... the body in Markdown ...
```

There are exactly two parts:

1. **The frontmatter** (between the `---` markers): a YAML header with metadata. This is what the agent framework reads to index and trigger the skill.
2. **The body** (everything after the closing `---`): Markdown instructions the model reads after the skill is triggered.

The frontmatter is the storefront sign. The body is the playbook. Everything in the next three lessons is about making both parts do their job well.

## Frontmatter Fields, One by One

Here is the full peer-matched frontmatter block used across the marketplace:

```yaml
---
name: my-skill-name               # lowercase, hyphens, max 64 chars
description: Use when <trigger>. <one-line behavior>.
version: 1.1.0
author: Hermes Agent
license: MIT
metadata:
  hermes:
    tags: [short, descriptive, tags]
    related_skills: [other-skill, another-skill]
---
```

What each field does:

- **`name`** is required. Lowercase letters and hyphens only, 64 characters max. This is the skill's unique ID. Pick something a human would search for.
- **`description`** is required, 1024 characters max. It must start with "Use when" and name the trigger class, not one specific task. We will drill this in Chapter 3.
- **`version`** is not enforced by the validator, but every peer skill has one. Use semantic versioning: `major.minor.patch`. Bump the patch for fixes, the minor for new sections or features, the major for breaking changes to the workflow.
- **`author`** credits the skill's author. Use your name or org.
- **`license`** declares how others may use and modify the skill. MIT is the common default in the marketplace.
- **`metadata.hermes.tags`** helps marketplace search and browsing. Three to six short, descriptive tags.
- **`metadata.hermes.related_skills`** names other skills this one works well with. This powers the "related" links on marketplace pages.

## The Validator's Hard Rules

The Hermes validator enforces a small set of non-negotiable rules. Break one and the skill will not load:

1. The file must start with `---` as the very first bytes. No leading blank line, no invisible characters.
2. The closing `---` must be followed by a newline, then the body.
3. The frontmatter must parse as a YAML mapping.
4. The `name` field must be present.
5. The `description` field must be present and no longer than 1024 characters.
6. There must be a non-empty body after the closing `---`.
7. The whole file must be under 100,000 characters (about 36k tokens). In practice, peer skills sit between 8,000 and 14,000 characters.

That is the entire enforcement surface. Everything else (version, author, license, metadata) is convention, but it is convention you should follow: a skill without version and author looks unfinished next to its peers.

## A Complete Minimal Example

Here is the smallest valid skill you could write:

```markdown
---
name: meeting-notes
description: Use when you need to turn rough meeting notes into a structured summary with action items.
version: 1.0.0
author: Your Name
license: MIT
metadata:
  hermes:
    tags: [notes, meetings, productivity]
    related_skills: []
---

# Meeting Notes

## Overview
Turns messy meeting notes into a structured summary: decisions, action items with owners, and open questions.

## When to Use
- After a meeting, when you paste raw notes and want a clean summary.
- Do not use for transcribing audio; that is a different skill.

## Procedure
1. Read the raw notes and identify decisions, action items, and open questions.
   - Done when: every action item has an owner named or marked "unassigned."
2. Write the summary under three headings: Decisions, Action Items, Open Questions.
   - Done when: all three headings are present, even if one is empty.

## Common Pitfalls
1. Inventing owners for action items. If no owner is named, write "unassigned."

## Verification Checklist
- [ ] Every action item has an owner or "unassigned"
- [ ] No content from the raw notes was dropped without being filed somewhere
```

Notice the pattern: triggers first, steps with completion criteria, pitfalls, checklist. This is the peer-matched shape you will see again and again.

lessons.title: The Body: Peer-Matched Structure
lessons.bodyMd:
## The Peer-Matched Body Structure

Across the marketplace, quality skills follow a predictable body structure. It is not enforced by the validator, but matching it makes your skill feel like a native citizen:

```
# <Title>

## Overview
One or two paragraphs: what the skill does and why.

## When to Use
- Bulleted triggers: the situations that should invoke this skill.
- "Don't use for:" counter-triggers: the look-alike tasks it does NOT cover.

## <Topic sections specific to the skill>
- Quick-reference tables are common.
- Code blocks with exact commands.
- Recipes for the skill's domain.

## Common Pitfalls
Numbered list of mistakes and their fixes.

## Verification Checklist
- [ ] Checkbox list of post-action verifications.
```

Not every section is mandatory, but `Overview` + `When to Use` + an actionable body + `Common Pitfalls` is the minimum. If you ship a skill missing those, reviewers will send it back.

## Why Each Section Exists

**Overview** gives the model its framing in two paragraphs. After reading this, the model should be able to answer "what am I being asked to do, in plain terms?" Keep it tight. If the overview needs three paragraphs, the skill is probably covering two jobs and should be split.

**When to Use** is the body-side twin of the description field. The description handles search matching; this section handles judgment. List the concrete trigger situations as bullets, and always include the "don't use for" counter-triggers. Counter-triggers are how you stop your skill from firing on look-alike tasks and stepping on a sibling skill's toes.

**The topic sections** are the meat. This is where commands, tables, decision trees, and recipes live. A strong convention: end each ordered step with a completion criterion, a checkable statement of how the agent knows the step is done. "Every modified file is accounted for" beats "summarize your changes." Completion criteria are the single highest-leverage writing habit in skill authoring, because they convert the model's tendency to rush into an explicit check it must pass.

**Common Pitfalls** captures failure modes with fixes. Number them. These are the lessons that took someone hours to learn; they are often the most valuable part of the skill. Real pitfalls from real skills look like this:

- Using bare `pip3 install` targets the system Python 3.9, which crashes on modern syntax. Always use the venv's `uv pip install` with `--python` pointed at the Hermes venv.
- Using the "create skill" tool for an in-repo skill writes to the user-local folder instead of the repo tree. Use `write_file` for in-repo creation.

**Verification Checklist** is the skill's definition of done, written as checkboxes. The model runs through it before finishing. A checklist with three to eight concrete items catches most premature-completion failures.

## Length Discipline

Peer skills land at 8,000 to 14,000 characters. If you are pushing past 20,000, that is a signal to split: keep the always-needed steps in `SKILL.md` and move bulky, branch-specific reference material into the skill folder's `references/` or `templates/` directories, pointing to them from the body. The body stays lean; the detail is one pointer away and loads only when needed.

This information hierarchy (always-needed in the body, sometimes-needed behind pointers) is what keeps the whole 369-skill marketplace cheap to run.

lessons.title: Conventions, Categories, and Placement
lessons.bodyMd:
## Where Skills Live: Directories and Categories

A skill is a folder, and the folder's location communicates scope. There are two homes:

1. **User-local:** `~/.hermes/skills/<optional-category>/<name>/SKILL.md`. Personal skills, not shared. These are yours alone; they follow you across projects on your machine.

2. **In-repo:** a committed folder like `skills/<category>/<name>/SKILL.md` inside a project repository. These ship with the package, are version-controlled, and are shared with everyone who clones the repo. This is the case the authoring skill in the marketplace documents most carefully.

Know which one you are writing, because the tooling differs. For example, in the Hermes agent framework, the `skill_manage(action='create')` tool writes to the user-local tree only. If you want to create an in-repo skill, you write the file directly with `write_file` and commit it with git. Using the wrong tool for the target tree is one of the most common beginner mistakes.

## Picking a Category

In-repo skills live under a category folder: `skills/<category>/<skill-name>/`. The marketplace's source repos already define categories like `software-development`, `productivity`, `research`, `devops`, `creative`, `data-science`, `email`, `social-media`, `smart-home`, `gaming`, `leisure`, and more.

The rule is simple: pick the closest existing category. Do not invent new top-level categories casually. A miscategorized skill is a skill nobody finds. When in doubt, list the category folder and read two or three peers first. Peers show you the tone, the structure, and the unwritten conventions of that category in a way no spec document can.

## Supporting Files in the Skill Folder

A skill folder can hold more than `SKILL.md`. The standard subdirectories are:

- **`references/`** : bulky or branch-specific reference material (API docs, schema dumps, long tables) that the body points to when needed.
- **`templates/`** : starter files the model copies and fills in.
- **`scripts/`** : helper scripts the model runs (test runners, validators, one-shot automations).
- **`assets/`** : images or other static files referenced by the body.

The body stays lean; these folders carry the weight. A body that says "run `scripts/run_tests.sh` and confirm all tests pass" is worth more than a body that pastes 200 lines of test procedure.

## LLM-Agnostic Conventions

A house rule across the marketplace: skills are written for any model, not one product. That shows up in small but important ways:

- Descriptions name multiple models when they say "instructs any AI model (Claude, GPT-4o, Gemini, Cursor)."
- Bodies reference standard commands and files rather than hidden product features.
- When a product-specific tool is unavoidable, it is named explicitly ("use `skill_manage(action='patch')`") rather than assumed.

The practical payoff: a skill you write today keeps working as models and tools change underneath it. Portability is a feature you get for free by writing in this style.

## Reading Checklist: The 60-Second Skill Review

Before you trust any skill, scan it in this order:

1. **Description:** does it start with "Use when" and name a clear trigger class?
2. **When to Use:** are there concrete triggers plus "don't use for" counter-triggers?
3. **Body:** are steps ordered with checkable completion criteria, or is it vague advice?
4. **Pitfalls:** are there numbered, specific failure modes with fixes, or generic warnings?
5. **Frontmatter:** version, author, license, tags, related skills all present?

If all five pass, the skill is probably worth installing. Chapter 3 goes deeper into what separates good skills from great ones.

lessons.title: The 8 Quality Principles
lessons.bodyMd:
## The North Star: Process Predictability

A skill exists to make an agent's process more predictable. Be careful with that word. Predictability does not mean identical output on every run; the model will (and should) adapt to each situation. It means the agent reliably follows the same useful discipline: the same checks, the same order, the same definition of done.

Every writing decision in this chapter serves that goal. When you evaluate a line in your skill, ask one question: **what behavior changes when the model reads this line?** If the answer is "nothing, it would do this anyway," cut the line. That single test eliminates most bad writing in skills.

## The Eight Quality Principles

These principles come from the marketplace's authoring skill. They are the review standard every skill is judged against:

1. **Optimize for process predictability.** Every line should change what the agent does. No-op lines get deleted, not polished.
2. **Choose the right context load.** The description is paid for on every turn, so keep it short and trigger-focused. Put details in the body or in linked reference files.
3. **Use an information hierarchy.** Always-needed steps go in `SKILL.md`. Branch-specific or bulky material goes in `references/`, `templates/`, or `scripts/` and is pointed to only when needed.
4. **End steps with completion criteria.** Each ordered step says how the agent knows it is done. Checkable and, when it matters, exhaustive.
5. **Co-locate rules with the concept they govern.** Keep a rule's definition, caveats, examples, and verification near each other. Do not scatter one idea across the file.
6. **Use strong leading words.** Prefer compact concepts the model already knows ("tracer bullet," "root cause," "regression test") over long repeated explanations. A good leading word saves tokens and anchors behavior.
7. **Prune duplication and no-ops.** Keep each meaning in one source of truth. Read sentence by sentence and ask whether each one changes behavior versus the model's default. If not, delete it.
8. **Watch for premature completion.** If agents tend to rush a step, first sharpen that step's completion criterion. Split the sequence only when later steps distract from doing the current step well.

## Applying the Principles: A Worked Example

Suppose you are writing a skill for deploying a static site. Here is a weak step:

> "Deploy the site carefully, making sure everything works."

It fails principle 1 (no behavior change: "carefully" means nothing to a model) and principle 4 (no completion criterion). Here is the strong version:

> "1. Deploy with `npm run deploy`. Done when: the deploy command exits 0 and the returned URL returns HTTP 200 for the homepage."

That step changes behavior: it names the exact command, and it gives the model a checkable test it must pass before moving on. Notice how short it is. Strength in skills comes from specificity, not length.

## The Editing Mindset

Good skills get shorter over time, not longer. When you add a rule, remove the old wording it replaces; do not layer advice forever. The marketplace calls accumulated stale advice "sediment," and it is one of the most common quality failures in older skills. Schedule a re-read of your skill every few months: if a line no longer changes behavior, it is sediment. Delete it.

In the next lesson you will apply these principles to the single most important sentence in any skill: the description.

lessons.title: Descriptions That Trigger Correctly
lessons.bodyMd:
## Your Description Is Your Storefront Sign

The description field is the only part of your skill the model reads on every single turn. It is how the agent framework decides whether to load your skill at all. A perfect body attached to a vague description is a playbook nobody ever opens.

The marketplace standard is rigid for a reason: descriptions start with **"Use when"** and describe the **trigger class**, not one specific task.

Compare:

- Weak: "A skill for Python packages."
- Weak: "Install requests with uv pip."
- Strong: "Use when you need to install and manage Python packages in the Hermes Agent virtual environment."

The strong version names the class of situations (installing and managing packages, in a specific environment). The weak ones name either nothing useful or one instance. The model matches descriptions against your request; it needs to see the class your request belongs to.

## The Formula

A strong description follows this formula:

**"Use when <trigger class>. <One line on the skill's distinctive behavior or scope.>"**

Real examples from the marketplace:

```yaml
description: "Use when you need to author in-repo SKILL.md: frontmatter, validator, structure, and writing-quality principles."
```

```yaml
description: "Use when you need to install and manage Python packages in the Hermes Agent virtual environment. Covers uv pip workflows, namespace-conflict recovery, disk space cleanup, and common packaging pitfalls."
```

Notice what they have in common: they name the trigger class first, then they name the distinctive coverage. They do not duplicate the body's step list; they summarize the territory.

## Rules for Descriptions

1. **Start with "Use when."** Every time. It is the marketplace convention and reviewers will flag you without it.
2. **Stay under 1024 characters.** In practice, stay far under: two sentences is the sweet spot. You are paying for these tokens on every turn.
3. **Name the trigger class, not the instance.** "Use when debugging database connection issues" beats "Use when Postgres fails."
4. **Do not duplicate the body.** The description summarizes; the body instructs. If your description is a list of the body's steps, shorten it.
5. **Name the environment when it matters.** "In the Hermes Agent virtual environment" disambiguates this skill from every other package-management guide in the library.

## Testing Your Description

Before you publish, run this test: give the description to a friend (or a fresh AI session) along with five task requests, only two of which your skill covers. Ask which requests would trigger the skill. If they pick the wrong ones, your description is either too broad (fires on everything) or too narrow (fires on nothing). Rewrite until the picks are obvious.

This test mirrors exactly how the agent framework behaves in production. The model is just a very fast reader of descriptions. Make its job easy.

lessons.title: Pitfalls That Kill Skills
lessons.bodyMd:
## The Four Killers

Most bad skills fail in one of four ways. Learn to spot them in other people's skills, and you will avoid them in your own.

### 1. No-Op Prose

No-op prose is advice the model would follow without being told. It reads like wisdom and does nothing.

- "Be careful when editing files."
- "Be thorough in your analysis."
- "Use best practices."

These lines fail the behavior-change test from Chapter 3, Lesson 1. The model is already careful and thorough by default; the sentence adds zero instruction. The fix is to replace each no-op with a checkable criterion or a stronger leading word:

- Weak: "Be careful when editing files."
- Strong: "Before editing, confirm the file's current contents with `read`. Done when: you can quote the exact lines you will change."

Every no-op you delete makes the remaining instructions stronger, because the model weights what is left more heavily.

### 2. Sediment

Sediment is stale advice that stays because adding felt safer than deleting. A skill accumulates it over versions: rule added in v1.2, contradicted softly in v1.4, never removed. The model now sees two rules that overlap and must guess which wins.

The fix is an editing discipline: when you add a rule, remove the old wording it replaces. When you review a skill, ask of each line: does this still change behavior today? Skills should get shorter and sharper over time, not longer.

### 3. Sprawl

Sprawl is too much always-visible material. A 25,000-character body that loads on every trigger costs tokens and buries the steps that matter. The fix is the information hierarchy from Lesson 1: always-needed steps stay in `SKILL.md`; bulky, branch-specific reference material moves into the skill folder's `references/` directory, pointed to from the body and loaded only when the task needs it. If your skill is pushing past 20,000 characters, that is the signal to split.

### 4. Premature Completion

Premature completion is the model declaring victory before the work is genuinely done. It is the most damaging failure because it looks like success: the model says "done" and moves on, but the checklist was never run.

The root cause is almost always a weak completion criterion. If agents tend to rush a step, first sharpen that step's criterion before you restructure anything. Compare:

- Weak: "3. Run the tests."
- Strong: "3. Run `scripts/run_tests.sh`. Done when: the script exits 0 with all tests passing; if any test fails, fix and re-run until green."

The strong version makes rushing impossible to justify, because "done" has a test attached. Split the sequence into more steps only when later steps genuinely distract from doing the current step well; most of the time, a sharper criterion is the fix.

## The Reviewer's Eye

When you review a skill (yours or someone else's), run this pass:

1. Read it line by line. For each line, ask: what behavior changes? Cut what fails.
2. Check every ordered step for a completion criterion. Sharpen the weak ones.
3. Scan for duplication: is any rule stated twice? Keep one source of truth.
4. Check length: past 20k characters, split into references.
5. Read the pitfalls section: are the failures specific with fixes, or generic warnings?

A skill that survives this pass is publish-ready. In Chapter 4 you will build one from scratch.

lessons.title: Pick a Workflow and Survey Peers
lessons.bodyMd:
## Start With a Workflow You Already Know

Do not start by inventing a skill. Start by noticing a workflow you repeat. Good first skills come from real repetition:

- The checklist you run before every deploy.
- The way you research a new topic (sources, note format, summary structure).
- How you triage your inbox or prep for a meeting.
- Your recipe for setting up a new project folder.

Pick one workflow that you do at least monthly, that has more than five steps, and that has at least one trap you have learned the hard way. That trap is the seed of your skill's pitfalls section, and it is often the most valuable part.

## Before You Write: Check for Duplicates

The marketplace already holds hundreds of skills. Before creating a new one, search the marketplace for siblings. A skill that duplicates an existing one will be flagged in review, and more importantly, two overlapping skills confuse the model's triggering.

If you find a close sibling, prefer extending it: propose an added section or a tightened pitfall rather than a narrow new skill. Create a new skill only when the workflow is genuinely distinct, or when the existing skill's trigger class does not cover your case.

## Survey Peers in the Target Category

Once you know your skill is new, find its category. Categories in the marketplace's source repos include `software-development`, `productivity`, `research`, `devops`, `creative`, `data-science`, and others. Pick the closest existing one; do not invent a new top-level category.

Then do what every experienced skill author does: list the category folder and read two or three peer `SKILL.md` files end to end. You are looking for:

- **Tone:** how formal or conversational are the instructions?
- **Structure:** which sections do peers include, and in what order?
- **Granularity:** how big is one step? How specific are the commands?
- **Conventions:** how do peers phrase completion criteria? How do they format pitfalls?

Peers are the unwritten spec. A skill that matches its category's conventions will feel native to reviewers and to the models that load it.

## Define the Trigger Class

Before writing a word of body, write the description's "Use when" sentence on a scratch pad. This forces you to define the skill's boundaries early, which prevents the most common structural failure: a skill that tries to cover two jobs.

Test the boundary with counter-triggers: name two look-alike tasks your skill does NOT cover. If you cannot name them, your skill is probably too broad. If the trigger class needs "and also" twice, you probably have two skills. Write both down; build one now.

You now have everything a first draft needs: a real workflow, no duplicate, a category with surveyed peers, and a crisp trigger class. In the next lesson you will write the frontmatter.

lessons.title: Draft the Frontmatter
lessons.bodyMd:
## Draft the Frontmatter First

Frontmatter first, body second. The frontmatter forces every scoping decision up front: the name is the ID, the description is the trigger, the tags are the discovery surface. Writing it first keeps the body honest.

Here is a worked example for a fictional first skill, a deploy checklist:

```yaml
---
name: static-site-deploy-checklist
description: "Use when you need to deploy a static site: pre-deploy checks, the deploy command, and post-deploy verification. Covers build validation, cache invalidation, and rollback steps."
version: 1.0.0
author: Your Name
license: MIT
metadata:
  hermes:
    tags: [deploy, static-site, checklist, verification]
    related_skills: []
---
```

Walk through each choice:

- **name:** lowercase, hyphens, under 64 characters. Descriptive enough to recognize in a list. `static-site-deploy-checklist` tells you the domain, the action, and the format.
- **description:** starts with "Use when," names the trigger class (deploying a static site), then one line on distinctive coverage (checks, deploy, verification, plus the named subtopics). Under 1024 characters, and in practice just two sentences.
- **version:** starts at `1.0.0`. You will bump it as the skill improves.
- **author / license:** your name and MIT unless you have a reason otherwise. Never ship without these; peers all have them and reviewers notice.
- **tags:** three to six short terms a marketplace browser would search for.
- **related_skills:** empty for now is fine, but revisit it after publishing when you discover siblings.

## Validate the Frontmatter Before You Continue

Run this quick check on your file before writing the body. It mirrors the validator's hard rules:

```python
import yaml, re, pathlib
content = pathlib.Path("SKILL.md").read_text()
assert content.startswith("---"), "must start with --- at byte 0"
m = re.search(r'\n---\s*\n', content[3:])
assert m, "closing --- not found"
fm = yaml.safe_load(content[3:m.start()+3])
assert "name" in fm and "description" in fm
assert len(fm["name"]) <= 64
assert len(fm["description"]) <= 1024
assert fm["description"].startswith("Use when")
assert len(content) <= 100_000
print("frontmatter OK")
```

If this passes, your skill will load. Everything from here is about quality, not validity.

## Common Frontmatter Mistakes

1. **A leading blank line before `---`.** The validator checks that the file starts with `---` at byte 0. One stray newline and the skill is rejected.
2. **A generic description.** "A deploy skill" will never trigger reliably. Name the trigger class.
3. **Name collisions.** Search the marketplace for your name before committing to it. Two skills with similar names and overlapping triggers split the model's confidence.
4. **Forgetting tags.** Tags are the marketplace's browsing surface. A skill with no tags is findable only by exact search.
5. **related_skills pointing at skills that do not exist** in the shared tree. User-local references do not resolve for other users. Link only to skills everyone can install.

Frontmatter done and validated. Next: the body.

lessons.title: Write the Body and Cut Ruthlessly
lessons.bodyMd:
## Write the Body: Overview, Triggers, Steps

With the frontmatter locking your scope, draft the body in the peer-matched order. Continuing the deploy-checklist example:

```markdown
# Static Site Deploy Checklist

## Overview
Deploys a static site safely: validates the build, deploys, verifies
the live site, and rolls back on failure. Built for teams that deploy
weekly and cannot afford a broken homepage.

## When to Use
- Deploying a static site to production.
- Re-deploying after a failed deploy (the rollback section applies).
- Do NOT use for: backend API deploys, database migrations, or
  mobile app releases. Those have their own skills.

## Procedure
1. Validate the build: run `npm run build`. 
   Done when: the build exits 0 with no errors.
2. Deploy: run `npm run deploy`.
   Done when: the command prints a live URL.
3. Verify: curl the live URL and confirm HTTP 200 on `/`.
   Done when: the homepage returns 200 and shows the expected title.
4. If verification fails, roll back: run `npm run rollback`.
   Done when: the previous deploy's URL returns 200 again.

## Common Pitfalls
1. Skipping the build validation because "it worked locally."
   Local and CI environments differ; always validate the real build.
2. Forgetting cache invalidation. If the CDN serves stale pages,
   purge the cache before declaring success.

## Verification Checklist
- [ ] Build exited 0
- [ ] Deploy printed a live URL
- [ ] Live URL returns HTTP 200 on `/`
- [ ] Rollback procedure confirmed available before deploying
```

## What to Notice in This Draft

**Every step ends with "Done when."** That is the completion-criterion habit from Chapter 3. It is the single most important sentence pattern in the whole file.

**The "Do NOT use for" line** draws the boundary. Backend deploys and migrations are look-alike tasks; naming them keeps this skill from firing where it does not belong.

**Pitfalls are specific with fixes.** Not "be careful," but the exact failure ("skipping validation because it worked locally") and why it fails (environments differ).

**The checklist is the definition of done.** The model runs it before finishing. Note the last item: "rollback procedure confirmed available before deploying." That is a seasoned operator's lesson, and it is exactly the kind of thing that makes a skill worth installing.

## The Information Hierarchy in Practice

Keep asking, per section: does the model need this on every run? The four procedure steps above are always-needed; they stay in the body. If your real workflow also includes a 40-row table of CDN cache TTLs per provider, that goes in `references/cdn-cache-ttls.md` and the body points to it: "If pages look stale, check `references/cdn-cache-ttls.md` for your provider's purge command." Lean body, rich references, cheap triggers.

## Draft, Then Cut

Write the full draft, then do a cutting pass with the behavior-change test: read each line and ask what the model would do differently because of it. Cut failures. Then check length: if you are past 20,000 characters, split reference material out. Aim for the peer range of 8,000 to 14,000 characters.

In the next lesson you will run the full validation and prepare the skill for publishing.

lessons.title: Validate, Trigger-Test, and Run Live
lessons.bodyMd:
## Run the Full Validation

Before a skill leaves your machine, it must pass three gates: the validator's hard rules, the quality review, and a live trigger test.

### Gate 1: The Validator

Extend the frontmatter check from the last lesson to the whole file:

```python
import yaml, re, pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("skills/<category>/<name>/SKILL.md")
content = p.read_text()
assert content.startswith("---")
m = re.search(r'\n---\s*\n', content[3:])
fm = yaml.safe_load(content[3:m.start()+3])
assert "name" in fm and "description" in fm
assert len(fm["description"]) <= 1024
assert len(content) <= 100_000
body = content[m.end()+3:].strip()
assert len(body) > 0, "body must be non-empty"
print(f"valid: {len(content)} chars, description {len(fm['description'])} chars")
```

### Gate 2: The Quality Review

Run the reviewer's pass from Chapter 3, Lesson 3:

1. Line by line: what behavior changes? Cut the failures.
2. Every ordered step has a checkable completion criterion.
3. No rule stated twice; one source of truth per meaning.
4. Under 20k characters, or reference material split out.
5. Pitfalls are specific with fixes, not generic warnings.
6. Description starts with "Use when" and names the trigger class.

### Gate 3: The Trigger Test

Give the skill's description (only the description) to a fresh AI session along with five realistic task requests, two of which the skill should cover. Ask which requests would trigger it. If the picks are wrong, the description is too broad or too narrow. Rewrite and retest. This is the cheapest test you will ever run and it catches the most common publishing failure.

## Test in a Real Session

Install the skill locally (user-local tree: `~/.hermes/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`) and use it for its real workflow once. Watch where the model hesitates or rushes:

- **Hesitation** usually means a step is missing context. Add the missing detail or a pointer to a reference file.
- **Rushing** usually means a weak completion criterion. Sharpen it until the model cannot justify skipping the check.

One real run teaches you more than five re-reads. Fix what you find, re-validate, bump the patch version.

## Know Your Target Tree

A final gotcha that bites beginners: the tool you use to create the skill depends on where it lives.

- **User-local skill** (`~/.hermes/skills/...`): personal, not shared. The framework's `skill_manage(action='create')` tool targets this tree.
- **In-repo skill** (`skills/<category>/<name>/` in a repo): committed and shared. Create it with `write_file` and commit with git; `skill_manage(action='create')` will NOT write here.

And one session note: the skill loader is initialized at session start, so a brand-new skill will not appear in `skills_list` until a fresh session. That is expected behavior, not a bug. Verify in a new session or by viewing the file directly.

Your skill now passes validation, quality review, triggering, and a live run. Chapter 5 takes it to the marketplace.

lessons.title: Packaging the Skill Folder
lessons.bodyMd:
## Packaging: What Goes in the Skill Folder

A publishable skill is a folder, not just a file. Here is the full layout:

```
<skill-name>/
  SKILL.md            # required: the playbook
  references/         # optional: bulky or branch-specific docs
  templates/          # optional: starter files the model fills in
  scripts/            # optional: helper scripts the model runs
  assets/             # optional: images or static files
```

`SKILL.md` is the only required file. Everything else is progressive disclosure: the body points to these folders only when the task needs them, so they cost nothing on triggers that do not.

Packaging rules that reviewers enforce:

1. **The body must stand alone.** A reviewer reading only `SKILL.md` should understand the full workflow. Reference files add depth; they must not contain steps the body forgot.
2. **Pointers must resolve.** Every `references/...`, `templates/...`, or `scripts/...` path named in the body must exist in the folder. A dangling pointer is a broken skill.
3. **Scripts must be runnable.** If the body says "run `scripts/run_tests.sh`," that script must exist, be executable, and do what the body claims. Reviewers will run it.
4. **No secrets in the package.** API keys, tokens, and credentials never ship in a skill. If the workflow needs a credential, the skill explains how the user provides it at runtime.

## The references/ Pattern, Worked

Suppose your deploy skill needs a long table of CDN purge commands per provider. The body stays lean:

```markdown
## Procedure
...
3. If pages look stale after deploy, purge the CDN cache using the
   command for your provider in `references/cdn-purge-commands.md`.
   Done when: a fresh curl shows the new content.
```

And `references/cdn-purge-commands.md` holds the full table. The model loads it only when a deploy actually looks stale. This is the information hierarchy doing its job: the 8k-character body triggers cheaply, and the 5k-character reference loads only on the branch that needs it.

## Pre-Publish Packaging Checklist

- [ ] `SKILL.md` passes the validator (frontmatter at byte 0, name and description present, description under 1024 chars, body non-empty, file under 100k chars)
- [ ] Body follows the peer-matched structure: Overview, When to Use (with counter-triggers), actionable steps with completion criteria, pitfalls, verification checklist
- [ ] Every pointer to `references/`, `templates/`, `scripts/`, or `assets/` resolves to a real file
- [ ] Scripts are executable and do what the body claims
- [ ] No credentials, tokens, or personal data anywhere in the folder
- [ ] Total size in the 8k-14k character peer range, or reference material split out with a reason

Package clean. Next: versioning.

lessons.title: Versioning Discipline
lessons.bodyMd:
## Semantic Versioning for Skills

The `version` field in your frontmatter is a promise to users: it tells them whether an update is safe to accept. Use semantic versioning, `major.minor.patch`:

- **Patch (1.0.0 to 1.0.1):** fixes. Typo corrections, a sharpened completion criterion, an added pitfall, a tightened trigger. Behavior improves; the workflow is unchanged.
- **Minor (1.0.0 to 1.1.0):** new capabilities. A new section, a new recipe, support for an additional tool in the same workflow. The skill does more, but existing behavior is backward compatible.
- **Major (1.0.0 to 2.0.0):** breaking changes. The workflow itself changed: steps reordered, a different tool required, a trigger class narrowed or widened. Users should re-read the skill before trusting the new version.

## Versioning Discipline in Practice

Two habits separate maintained skills from abandoned ones:

**1. Bump on every publish.** Never push an edited skill with the old version number. Users and the marketplace diff versions to decide whether to update; a silent change with no bump is invisible and untrustworthy. Even a one-line pitfall fix earns a patch bump.

**2. Keep a changelog.** You do not need a formal file, but the skill's history should be legible. In a repo-backed skill this is the git log. For marketplace listings, the publish notes for each version should say what changed in one line: "1.1.0: added rollback recipe for failed deploys." One line per version is enough; it is the difference between a skill users update confidently and one they pin forever.

## When to Split Instead of Bump

Versioning has a limit: if your "minor update" doubles the skill's size or adds a second trigger class, you do not have an update. You have a second skill wearing the first one's name. Split it:

- Extract the new workflow into its own skill with its own "Use when" description.
- Link them with `metadata.hermes.related_skills` on both sides.
- Bump the original to note the split in its publish notes.

The marketplace rewards focused skills. A 10k-character skill with one crisp trigger beats a 25k-character skill with three fuzzy ones, because the model triggers the focused one reliably and hesitates on the sprawling one.

## The Maintenance Mindset

Publishing is not the end; it is the start of maintenance. Good skill authors:

- Re-read their skill every few months and cut sediment (stale lines that no longer change behavior).
- Watch for user reports of misfires (triggered when it should not have) or misses (not triggered when it should have). Both are description problems; fix the description first.
- Update `related_skills` as the marketplace grows and siblings appear.

A skill that gets shorter and sharper over time is a skill users keep installed. In the final lesson you will walk the actual publishing steps.

lessons.title: Publishing Steps and Discovery
lessons.bodyMd:
## The Publishing Steps

Publishing a skill to the LetsVibeAI marketplace takes a packaged, validated skill and makes it discoverable. The exact submission flow lives on the marketplace site, but the author's side of the process is the same everywhere:

1. **Final validation.** Re-run the validator from Chapter 4, Lesson 4 on the exact folder you will submit. Validate the artifact, not a draft.
2. **Write the listing summary.** The marketplace shows your description plus your tags. Re-read both with fresh eyes: would a stranger understand what triggers this skill and what it does? This is your last chance to fix a vague description.
3. **Choose the category.** Pick the closest existing marketplace category (mirroring the repo categories: software-development, productivity, research, and so on). Do not invent a new category for one skill.
4. **Set related skills.** Name two or three skills yours pairs with. Good related links are the marketplace's best discovery feature; they turn one install into a working set. Only link to skills that exist in the shared tree, never to your user-local-only skills.
5. **Submit and respond to review.** Expect feedback on the first submission: a tightened description, a sharper completion criterion, a missing counter-trigger. This is normal and it makes the skill better. Address each note, bump the patch version, resubmit.

## Discovery: How Users Find Your Skill

Three surfaces bring users to your skill, and you control all three:

- **Search** reads your name, description, and tags. This is why the "Use when" description and three to six honest tags matter so much.
- **Categories** group your skill with its peers. A correct category puts you next to the skills users already trust.
- **Related skills** (`metadata.hermes.related_skills`) power the "pairs well with" links. Cross-referencing is a growth loop: when a popular skill links to yours, you inherit its audience.

There is a fourth surface you do not control: the model's own triggering. When your description is crisp, the agent framework surfaces your skill exactly when the user's task matches. That is the ultimate distribution channel, and it is earned entirely in the two sentences of your description.

## After Publishing: The First 30 Days

1. **Watch for misfires and misses.** If users report the skill firing on the wrong tasks, the description is too broad. If it never fires, the description is too narrow or the trigger class is mislabeled. Fix the description first; it is the cheapest change with the largest effect.
2. **Collect pitfalls from the field.** Real users will hit failure modes you never imagined. Each one is a future entry in your Common Pitfalls section and a patch version bump.
3. **Link new siblings.** As the marketplace grows, new skills will appear that pair with yours. Update `related_skills` on both sides.

## The Flywheel You Just Joined

Step back and see the whole picture. You learned a workflow, captured it as a skill, validated it, published it, and now strangers' AI agents follow your discipline every time the trigger matches. Every pitfall you documented saves someone an hour. Every completion criterion you sharpened prevents a silent failure.

That is the Hermes idea in one sentence: **workflows worth repeating are worth packaging.** The marketplace is 369 skills today because hundreds of builders each packaged one workflow they knew cold. Yours is next.

Go build it.
